Inquire means to seek information by asking, or to look into something carefully to find out more about it. Think of it as a deliberate, purposeful act of wanting to know something — and then doing something about it.

It is essentially a more formal, slightly elevated way of saying "ask" or "look into." Whenever you use "inquire," you signal that the act of asking or investigating is thoughtful and intentional, not just casual chatter.

The verb "inquire" works in two closely related but distinct ways:

1. To Ask for Information

This is the everyday sense. You inquire about something when you want to learn a specific piece of information by asking someone.

"She walked into the office to inquire about the job opening."
"He called the hospital to inquire about visiting hours."
"The customer inquired whether the product was available in blue."

Notice that in all these cases, a person has a question, goes to a source, and asks it directly. It is more deliberate and polite-sounding than simply saying "asked."

2. To Investigate Something Thoroughly

This is the deeper, more serious sense. Here, "inquire" means to look carefully into a situation, issue, or matter — often to uncover the truth or understand the full picture. This is commonly used in formal, official, or professional settings.

"The government set up a committee to inquire into the causes of the accident."
"Journalists began to inquire into the company's financial practices."
"The police inquired into the events leading up to the crime."

Here, "inquire" is not just asking one question — it means conducting a thorough examination or investigation.

There is a third, more specific pattern worth knowing. To inquire after someone means to ask about their health, well-being, or current situation — usually out of genuine care or politeness.

"My neighbor called to inquire after my mother, who had been unwell."
"He stopped by to inquire after the old man's health."

This usage is more common in formal or old-fashioned English, but you will still encounter it in books, letters, and polite conversation.

"Inquire" sits firmly on the formal side of the language spectrum. It is the word you would use in professional emails, official documents, journalism, legal contexts, and academic writing — rather than in casual everyday conversation with friends.

Compare these two sentences — they mean the same thing, but feel very different:

  • Casual: "I asked about the price."
  • Formal: "I inquired about the price."

Neither is wrong. But "inquire" carries a sense of seriousness, professionalism, and deliberate action that "ask" does not always carry.
Common Phrases and Patterns at a Glance

Here are the main patterns "inquire" appears in, with a note on what each one signals:

Inquire about something → Ask for information on a specific topic.

"Please inquire about the schedule at the front desk."

Inquire into something → Investigate or examine something in depth.

"The board will inquire into the allegations of misconduct."

Inquire after someone → Ask about a person's health or well-being.

"She inquired after your recovery."

Inquire of someone → Ask a particular person directly (slightly old-fashioned but still used).

"You may inquire of the manager if you need further assistance."

"Please inquire within" → A well-known phrase on signs, meaning "come inside and ask for more details."
How It Differs From Similar Words

Ask is the plain, everyday word. "Inquire" does the same job but feels more formal and deliberate. You would rarely say "inquire" to a friend in a text message, but you would use it in a professional email or a news report.

Investigate goes further than "inquire." If "inquire" is asking questions and looking into things, "investigate" is a deep, systematic, and often official process of uncovering facts. Inquiring can be the first step before investigating.

Question implies actively asking someone in a pointed or direct way — sometimes with doubt or pressure behind it. "Inquire" feels more neutral and open.
A Few More Natural Examples in Context

• The student inquired whether the library had the book in stock.
  • After the explosion, authorities inquired into the safety procedures at the factory.
  • I am writing to inquire about the status of my application.
  • She inquired after her old professor, whom she had not seen in years.
  • If you wish to book a table, please inquire at the reception.
  • The journalist spent months inquiring into the corruption scandal.

Inquire means to deliberately seek information — either by asking someone a question, or by investigating a matter more carefully — and it carries a formal, thoughtful tone that sets it apart from the simpler word "ask."
A Note on Spelling: Inquire vs. Enquire

You may sometimes see the spelling enquire (with an e). In American English, "inquire" is the standard spelling for all uses. In British English, both spellings exist, and some writers use "enquire" for general asking and "inquire" for formal investigation — but even in Britain, "inquire" is widely accepted for all purposes. If you are writing in American English, always use inquire.
